尺八傳統上以竹製成，琴身取用竹根端部，吹口（歌口）由竹材自然斜切形成。現代亦有塑: The shakuhachi is traditionally made of bamboo, the body taken from the root end, and the mouthpiece (utaguchi) is formed by a natural diagonal cut in the bamboo. Modern versions are also made of plastic, ebonite, anodised aluminium and hardwood. The bore of a bamboo shakuhachi is coated in several layers of ji paste, which the source describes as containing tonoko powder and another material for which no Chinese name is given, finished outside with lacquer. The source does not describe the materials of the other parts or of the inlaid mouthpiece.
尺八是日本氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 421.111.12: The shakuhachi is a Japanese aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.111.12, an end-blown vertical flute. It is traditionally made from the root end of bamboo, with five fingerholes on the body tuned to a minor pentatonic scale; the player blows against the edge of the mouthpiece, then controls pitch and timbre by covering the holes, by the blowing angle and by changes of embouchure. Fuke Zen monks used it to practise suizen, and it is also used in ensembles with koto, biwa and shamisen, in folk music, in jazz and in modern pieces.
尺八源自中國竹笛，7或8世紀傳入日本。古代尺八又稱雅樂尺八，用於雅樂，10世紀失: The shakuhachi comes from the Chinese bamboo flute and reached Japan in the seventh or eighth century. The ancient shakuhachi, also called gagaku shakuhachi, was used in gagaku; it was lost in the tenth century, and only eight instruments survive in the Shōsōin, with no scores to consult. The fifteenth century saw the hitoyogiri shakuhachi, which flourished in the seventeenth century and then fell out of use as the Fuke shakuhachi rose. In the sixteenth century Japan developed the Fuke shakuhachi, longer and thicker than the older type, with better volume, range, scale and timbre; in the medieval period it was tied to the suizen practice of Fuke sect monks and became the shakuhachi as generally known today.
尺八的聆聽場合包括宗教與世俗演出。普化禪僧以尺八修習吹禪，並演奏原創禪樂；世俗方: The shakuhachi is heard on both religious and secular occasions. Fuke Zen monks practise suizen with it and play their own Zen music; on the secular side, professional players play in ensemble with koto, biwa and shamisen, and it is also used in folk music, jazz and modern works. The traditional honkyoku value layers of timbre, and some honkyoku, especially those of the Nezasa school (Kinpū-ryū), suit a longer shakuhachi. The source gives no composers or particular titles, so no works are listed.
尺八音色蒼涼悠遠，具有深沉而內斂的暗沉質感，散發著禪意的空靈韻味。其音域寬廣，從: The shakuhachi has a bleak, far-carrying timbre, with a deep, restrained, dark quality and an air of Zen emptiness. Its range is wide: thick and sinewy in the low register, warm and full in the middle, then clear and sharp at the top, with distinct layers. Because it sounds through the vibration of an edge and its resonating cavity is a hollow bamboo tube, its sound has a natural warmth and resonance. Beside the bright clarity of the Western flute, the shakuhachi is more composed and restrained; beside the saxophone, its timbre is more ethereal. Its distinctive breath technique and changes of fingering give it a highly expressive musical language: it can play a long, sinuous melody and can also convey a bleak, sombre mood.
